title: A Holy People at the Table: Food Laws and the Tithe
summary: Because Israel is God's holy people, they must not gash themselves or shave their heads in mourning as the nations did. Moses lists the animals, fish, and birds Israel may and may not eat, forbids eating an animal that died on its own, and bans cooking a young goat in its mother's milk. The chapter ends with the tithe: a tenth of the harvest is to be eaten in joy at the sanctuary, and every third year it is stored in the towns for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.
story: Chapters 12 and 13 guarded Israel's worship from the practices of Canaan and the voices that would lead them away. Chapter 14 carries that same concern into daily life: grief, meals, and harvest. The chapter opens and closes its first half with the same claim, “you are a people holy to the LORD your God” (verse 2; compare verse 21), which is the reason for everything in it. Holiness is not confined to the sanctuary; it reaches the family table and the funeral. The tithe at the chapter's end ties Israel's food back to the chosen place of chapter 12 and to the care for the vulnerable that runs through the law code.
historical:
The list of clean and unclean animals appears in fuller form in Leviticus 11, and the two lists overlap closely. Deuteronomy's version is shorter and addresses ordinary households rather than priests. Many of the bird names in verses 12 to 18 are rare words whose exact meaning is uncertain, and translations differ on several of them; the identifications in the English text are the translators' best judgments. For the question of how Deuteronomy relates in date to Leviticus and the other books of the Pentateuch, see the note on Deuteronomy 5.

Archaeology offers one striking pattern. Pig bones are common at many Late Bronze and Iron Age sites in the southern Levant, such as Philistine cities on the coast, but are rare or absent at Iron Age sites in the central highlands where Israelites settled. Some archaeologists have taken this as evidence that avoiding pork was an early marker of Israelite identity, though others caution that diet also depended on environment and economy.
cultural:
Cutting the body and shaving the head were common mourning rites in the ancient Near East. Texts from Ugarit describe the god El gashing himself in grief for the dead Baal, and the prophets of Baal cut themselves in their ritual on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:28). Such rites could be tied to the cult of the dead or to appeasing the gods. Israel was to grieve, but not in ways that marred the body or borrowed from those practices, because they were “sons of the LORD your God” (verse 1).

The command not to cook a young goat in its mother's milk (verse 21, also in Exodus 23:19 and 34:26) has puzzled readers for centuries. The medieval Jewish scholar Maimonides thought it opposed a pagan ritual, and a text from Ugarit was once read as describing such a rite, though that reading is now widely doubted. Others see it as a law of compassion, refusing to mix the source of life with the death of the young. Rabbinic tradition developed from it the Jewish practice of separating meat and dairy. The tithe, a tenth of the yearly produce, was a common form of offering in the ancient world, owed to kings or temples. Here it becomes a family feast before God and, every third year, a food bank for those with no land of their own.
literary: The chapter has two parts joined by the theme of eating. Verses 1 to 21 are bracketed by the statement that Israel is a holy people (verses 2 and 21) and organized, as in Leviticus 11, by the realms of creation: land animals, water creatures, birds, and flying insects. Each category is given a simple test (split hooves and chewing the cud, fins and scales) followed by exceptions. Verses 22 to 29 turn to the tithe, with two provisions: an annual tithe eaten at the sanctuary, with a practical allowance for those who live far away, and a third-year tithe kept in the towns for the needy. The word eat appears seventeen times.

outline.t: Do not mourn like the nations
Clean and unclean birds and flying insects
Carcasses and a young goat in its mother's milk
The yearly tithe, eaten with joy before God
The third-year tithe for the Levite and the needy

doctrines.note: Israel's holiness is a gift before it is a task: they are God's sons and his treasured possession. The food laws and mourning customs express that identity in the most ordinary acts, teaching that every part of life belongs to God.

The law turns giving into worship. The tithe is eaten “in the presence of the LORD your God” with rejoicing (verses 23 and 26), “so that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always.” Giving back to God is framed as a feast and a lesson in reverence.

Israel is called God's children (verse 1), a title that explains why they must not grieve as the nations do. The third-year tithe extends the household's table to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.

words.note: Qadosh, holy, set apart. It describes what belongs to God and is marked off from common use. Israel is a holy people (verses 2 and 21) not because they are morally better than others but because God chose them for himself. The laws that follow show what that belonging looks like in daily life.

Tame, unclean. In the Old Testament uncleanness is not the same as sin or dirt. It is a ritual status that affects access to worship. Unclean animals were not evil; they were simply not to be eaten by Israel, a boundary that marked Israel as distinct.

Ma'aser, tithe, a tenth. Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek (Genesis 14:20), and Jacob vowed a tenth to God (Genesis 28:22). In Deuteronomy the tithe is eaten by the worshiper at the sanctuary and shared with the needy, a different emphasis from Numbers 18, where it supports the Levites.

christ: Jesus taught that what enters a person from outside cannot defile them, and Mark adds that in saying this he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:18-19). Peter's vision in Acts 10, in which he was told to eat animals that the law called unclean, taught him that God was welcoming Gentiles into his people without requiring them to become Jews first. The early church recognized that the food laws had marked Israel off from the nations, and that in Christ the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile had come down (Ephesians 2:14). What the food laws taught remains: God's people are holy, set apart for him in every area of life. The New Testament now locates that holiness in the heart and in love rather than in the menu. Jesus also affirmed the tithe while rebuking those who tithed their herbs and neglected justice, mercy, and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23).

hard.q: Why were some animals unclean, and do the food laws still apply?
hard.a:
Deuteronomy gives no reason for the particular list, and interpreters have offered many. The hygiene view holds that unclean animals were more likely to carry disease, though this does not explain every case. The cultic view notes that some unclean animals, like the pig, were used in pagan rituals. The symbolic view, associated with the anthropologist Mary Douglas in Purity and Danger (1966), argues that clean animals fit the ordinary categories of their realm (land, sea, sky) and unclean ones mixed or crossed those categories, so that the food laws taught wholeness and order. Others see the laws mainly as a boundary marker, a daily reminder that Israel was set apart, whatever the reason for each animal. These views are not mutually exclusive.

On whether the laws still apply, Jewish tradition continues to observe them as part of the covenant with Israel. Most Christian traditions hold that Jesus and the apostles declared all foods clean for believers (Mark 7:19; Acts 10; Romans 14), so that the food laws are no longer binding, though they still teach holiness. Some Christian groups, such as Seventh-day Adventists, continue to avoid unclean meats. The apostolic council in Acts 15 asked Gentile believers to observe a few restrictions, including abstaining from blood, out of care for their Jewish brothers and sisters.

questions: Israel was to grieve, but not in the ways the nations did. How does faith in God shape the way you grieve?
The food laws made holiness a matter of daily meals. What ordinary habits in your life could be reminders that you belong to God?
The tithe was both a feast before God and provision for the poor. How does your giving reflect both joy and care for others?
